records.source: Ὦ ἀνόητοι Γαλάται, τίς ὑμᾶς ἐβάσκανεν, οἷς κατ’ ὀφθαλμοὺς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς προεγράφη ἐσταυρωμένος;
records.gloss: O foolish Galatians, who you bewitched, to whom before eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed having been crucified?
pieces: You foolish Galatians! Who has put you under a spell? Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was set out in full view before your eyes as the crucified one.

L.1: O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was publicly portrayed as crucified?

R.1: You foolish people of Galatia! Who has put a spell on you? It was made so plain to you that Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was crucified. It was as if you had seen it with your own eyes.

decisions.choice: foolish: failing to think, not lacking intelligence
decisions.reason: ἀνόητος describes people who do not use the understanding they have. Paul is not insulting their minds; he is shocked that they have not thought through what they already know. He repeats the word in verse 3.

decisions.choice: bewitched: a figure of speech for being led astray as if by a spell
alternatives: a claim that real sorcery was used
decisions.reason: βασκαίνω was used of casting a spell, often through the "evil eye" that people of the time feared. Paul uses it as an image: the change in the Galatians is so strange that it looks as though someone has put them under a spell. The image fits the "eyes" that follow: they had seen Christ crucified, yet someone has drawn their gaze away.

decisions.choice: publicly portrayed: set before them as plainly as a public notice
alternatives: written about beforehand, as in the prophets
decisions.reason: προγράφω was used of notices posted in public. Paul's preaching had made the crucifixion so vivid that it was as though they saw it. The same verb can mean "written beforehand" (Romans 15:4), but "before your eyes" points to a public display, not to prophecy.

decisions.choice: crucified: Christ remains the crucified one
alternatives: a reference only to the past event
decisions.reason: ἐσταυρωμένος is a perfect participle: the crucifixion happened once, but its effect stands, and Christ is presented as the one who was crucified. Everything Paul argues in this chapter rests on what the cross did (verse 13).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: put you under a spell; set out in full view; as if you had seen it with your own eyes (R)
decisions.reason: "Bewitched" is an old-fashioned word, so Balanced and Readable use "spell". Readable breaks the sentence and explains the picture of a public display (meaning note m3).

records.heading: Faith or works of the law?

records.source: τοῦτο μόνον θέλω μαθεῖν ἀφ’ ὑμῶν, ἐξ ἔργων νόμου τὸ πνεῦμα ἐλάβετε ἢ ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως;
records.gloss: This only I want to learn from you: by works of law the Spirit did you receive, or by hearing of faith?
pieces: Tell me just this one thing: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by faith in what you heard?

L.2: This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of [the] law, or by [the] hearing of faith?

R.2: I want you to answer just one question. Did you receive the Spirit because you did what the law commands? Or was it because you heard the message and put your faith in it?

decisions.choice: the Spirit: God's Holy Spirit, given to them when they first believed
decisions.reason: Paul appeals to what the Galatians experienced: they received the Spirit of God (4:6) at the start of their life as believers. That gift is his evidence that God had already accepted them before anyone asked them to keep the law.

decisions.choice: works of the law: doing what the law of Moses requires
alternatives: only the ceremonial parts of the law
decisions.reason: The law is the law God gave through Moses. In this letter the question is above all circumcision, the food laws and the special days (2:3, 2:12, 4:10), the practices that marked Jews out from Gentiles, but Paul's argument covers keeping the law as a whole (3:10, 5:3).

decisions.choice: hearing with faith: they heard the message and believed it
alternatives: the message that calls for faith
decisions.reason: ἀκοή can mean the act of hearing or the message heard, and πίστις can mean the believer's faith or the content believed. So the phrase may mean "hearing accompanied by faith" or "the message that brings faith". Either way the contrast is between doing what the law requires and receiving God's message by believing it. We take the first, which matches "Abraham believed" in verse 6, and give the other in a footnote.

decisions.choice: works of [the] law (L); works of the law (B); doing what the law commands (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep Paul's phrase so the reader can follow it through the letter. Readable says plainly what it refers to.

decisions.choice: faith in what you heard (B); heard the message and put your faith in it (R)
decisions.reason: "Hearing of faith" is not natural English. Balanced and Readable give the sense chosen in meaning note m3 and keep the key word "faith".

records.source: οὕτως ἀνόητοί ἐστε;
records.gloss: So foolish are you?
pieces: Are you really that foolish?

R.3: How can you be so foolish?

decisions.choice: a question of astonishment
decisions.reason: The question expects no answer. With οὕτως ("so") Paul repeats the word "foolish" from verse 1 and voices his amazement at what they are doing.

records.source: ἐναρξάμενοι πνεύματι νῦν σαρκὶ ἐπιτελεῖσθε;
records.gloss: Having begun in Spirit, now in flesh are you being completed?
pieces: You made your start by the Spirit; are you now going to reach the goal by the flesh?

L.3: Having begun by [the] Spirit, are you now being brought to completion by [the] flesh?

R.3: You began your new life by the Spirit. Do you now think you can finish it by your own human effort?

decisions.choice: flesh: human effort, what people can do in their own strength
decisions.reason: Set against the Spirit, σάρξ here means human beings acting on their own, without God. Paul is thinking of circumcision, a rite performed on the body, and of law-keeping as the way to complete their standing with God (6:12-13). Later in the letter the same word means the sinful human self (5:16-24).

decisions.choice: by the Spirit, by the flesh: the means by which the life is begun and finished
alternatives: in the sphere of the Spirit and of the flesh
decisions.reason: The two nouns stand without a preposition and say how each stage is brought about. Paul's question is whether the life the Spirit began can be completed by a different power.

decisions.choice: brought to completion: reaching the goal of the Christian life
decisions.reason: ἐπιτελέω means to bring something to its end or goal. Its form can be read as passive ("are you being completed") or as middle ("are you completing it"); the sense is the same. The contrast with "begun" shows that Paul has the whole course of their life with God in view.

decisions.choice: your new life; your own human effort
decisions.reason: Readable names what was begun and says what "flesh" means here (meaning note m1).

records.source: τοσαῦτα ἐπάθετε εἰκῇ;
records.gloss: So many things did you experience in vain?
pieces: Did you go through so much for nothing?

L.4: Did you experience so many things in vain?

R.4: Have all the things that happened to you been for nothing?

decisions.choice: experienced: all they went through as believers, good and hard
decisions.reason: πάσχω usually means to suffer, and the Galatians may have been persecuted when they believed. But the verses around it speak of the Spirit and of miracles (verses 2-5), not of persecution, and the letter never mentions their suffering. So it may mean "experience" in a good sense. Both senses fit what Paul is asking: has all of it been wasted?

decisions.choice: experience (L); go through (B); things that happened to you (R)
decisions.reason: These words leave room for both readings in meaning note m1.

records.source: εἴ γε καὶ εἰκῇ.
records.gloss: If indeed also in vain.
pieces: If it really was for nothing.

R.4: I hope it was not all for nothing!

decisions.choice: a note of hope: Paul does not believe it was really in vain
alternatives: a warning: it will prove to be in vain if they turn to the law
decisions.reason: εἴ γε limits what has just been said: "if it really was in vain". Paul is probably holding out hope that it was not, as he does in 5:10. The other reading hears a warning: all they experienced will be wasted if they go on as they are. The two are close, and Paul may mean both.

decisions.choice: I hope it was not all for nothing
alternatives: if indeed it was for nothing
decisions.reason: Readable states the hope that the short phrase implies (meaning note m1). Literal and Balanced keep Paul's open wording.

records.source: ὁ οὖν ἐπιχορηγῶν ὑμῖν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ἐνεργῶν δυνάμεις ἐν ὑμῖν ἐξ ἔργων νόμου ἢ ἐξ ἀκοῆς πίστεως;
records.gloss: The [one] therefore supplying to you the Spirit and working miracles among you, by works of law or by hearing of faith?
pieces: So then, does God give you the Spirit and work miracles among you because of works of the law, or because of faith in what you heard?

L.5: So then, the one who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you, [does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} do it] by works of [the] law, or by [the] hearing of faith?

R.5: God gives you the Spirit and does miracles among you. Does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} do this because you do what the law commands? Or is it because you heard the message and put your faith in it?

decisions.choice: the one who supplies the Spirit: God
alternatives: the apostle or another human teacher
decisions.reason: Only God gives the Spirit and works miracles. The present participles say that he goes on doing so among the Galatians; it is not only a past event.

decisions.choice: supplies: gives generously
decisions.reason: ἐπιχορηγέω was used of providing fully for a need. God's giving of the Spirit is generous and continuing.

decisions.choice: miracles among you
decisions.reason: δύναμις in the plural means acts of power, miracles. ἐν ὑμῖν can mean "among you" or "within you"; Paul is appealing to things they had all seen happen in their churches.

decisions.choice: the same choice as in verse 2: works of the law or hearing with faith
decisions.reason: Paul repeats the question of verse 2 word for word, now about what God is still doing among them. The phrase "hearing of faith" is read the same way as there.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God, who is meant (meaning note m1).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: A pronoun for God follows the reader's setting.

decisions.choice: works of [the] law (L); works of the law (B); do what the law commands (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2.

records.source: καθὼς Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσεν τῷ θεῷ, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.
records.gloss: Just as Abraham believed the God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.
pieces: So it was with Abraham: he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.

L.6: Just as Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

R.6: It was the same with Abraham. He believed God, and because he believed, God accepted him as righteous.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Genesis 15:6
alternatives: a general summary of Abraham's life
decisions.reason: Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 in the words of its Greek translation, without an introductory formula. God had promised Abraham offspring as many as the stars, and Abraham believed him. Paul uses the same verse in Romans 4:3.

decisions.choice: just as: the Galatians' experience matches Abraham's
alternatives: a new argument, unconnected with verses 2-5
decisions.reason: καθώς ties Abraham to what Paul has just said: the Galatians received the Spirit by believing, just as Abraham was accepted by believing. The Jewish teachers in Galatia probably pointed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17); Paul points to Genesis 15, which comes before it.

decisions.choice: reckoned: counted, entered to his account
decisions.reason: λογίζομαι is a word from bookkeeping: something is entered to a person's account. God counted Abraham's believing as righteousness. The "it" is his believing.

decisions.choice: righteousness: a right standing with God
decisions.reason: Righteousness here is the standing of one who is in the right before God, as the word "justify" in verses 8 and 11 shows.

decisions.choice: reckoned (L); counted (B)
decisions.reason: Both keep the picture of an entry in an account.

decisions.choice: because he believed, God accepted him as righteous
alternatives: it was counted to him as righteousness
decisions.reason: Readable says who did the counting and what "it" refers to (meaning note m3). It keeps the key word in the form "righteous".

records.source: Γινώσκετε ἄρα ὅτι οἱ ἐκ πίστεως, οὗτοι υἱοί εἰσιν Ἀβραάμ.
records.gloss: Know then that those of faith, these sons are of Abraham.
pieces: You can see, then, that the people of faith are the ones who are Abraham's {{gender:children|sons}}.

L.7: Know, then, that those [who are] of faith, these are {{gender:children|sons}} of Abraham.

R.7: So understand this: the people who live by faith are Abraham's real {{gender:children|sons}}.

decisions.choice: an instruction: know, understand
decisions.reason: Γινώσκετε can be a command or a statement of what they know. Either way Paul draws a conclusion from Genesis 15:6, as ἄρα ("then") shows.

decisions.choice: those of faith: people whose standing with God comes from faith
alternatives: people who are loyal or faithful
decisions.reason: The phrase describes people by where their life with God comes from. Paul sets them against "those who are of works of the law" in verse 10.

decisions.choice: sons of Abraham: his true descendants and heirs
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures being someone's υἱός means belonging to his family, sharing his character and inheriting what is his. The word gives the status of a son and heir, which Paul applies to men and women alike (3:28-29). Those who believe, as Abraham did, are his family, whether or not they are descended from him.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The word means men and women here (meaning note m3), so it follows the gender setting.

decisions.choice: live by faith; real
decisions.reason: Readable explains the short phrase "those of faith" and adds "real" to bring out the contrast with physical descent (meaning note m3).

records.heading: Abraham's children by faith

records.source: προϊδοῦσα δὲ ἡ γραφὴ ὅτι ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοῖ τὰ ἔθνη ὁ θεὸς προευηγγελίσατο τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ὅτι Ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη.
records.gloss: Having foreseen and the Scripture that by faith justifies the Gentiles the God, proclaimed the gospel beforehand to the Abraham: Will be blessed in you all the nations.
pieces: Scripture saw in advance that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and so it announced the gospel ahead of time to Abraham: "In you all the nations will be blessed."

L.8: And the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, proclaimed the gospel beforehand to Abraham: "All the nations will be blessed in you."

R.8: Long before, Scripture looked ahead and saw that God would put the Gentiles right with {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} by faith. So it told Abraham the good news ahead of time: "Because of you, all the nations will be blessed."

decisions.choice: Scripture foresaw: God speaking in Scripture
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of Scripture as if it could see ahead and preach. He means God, who spoke the words recorded in it and knew what he would do (compare 3:22 and Romans 9:17).

decisions.choice: God declares a person to be in the right before him: acquitted and accepted
alternatives: a person proves to be good
decisions.reason: δικαιόω is a word from the law court: the judge declares someone to be in the right. Here God is the judge, and the person he justifies is accepted by him and stands in the right before him (2:16). It is a verdict God gives, not a reward for good conduct.

decisions.choice: a quotation of God's promise in Genesis 12:3 and 18:18
alternatives: a general blessing on Abraham alone
decisions.reason: The words come from God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 ("in you all the families of the earth will be blessed") and 18:18 ("all the nations of the earth"). Paul calls that promise the gospel announced in advance: already then God meant to bless the Gentiles.

decisions.choice: nations and Gentiles: the same word
decisions.reason: ἔθνος means both "nations" and "Gentiles", the peoples other than Israel. Paul's point depends on it: the nations promised a blessing in Genesis are the Gentiles God now justifies by faith.

decisions.choice: in you: through Abraham, and as people joined to him
decisions.reason: The nations are blessed because of Abraham and by sharing in the blessing given to him; verse 9 says they are blessed "with" him. The promise comes to them in Christ (verse 14).

decisions.choice: justifies / would justify (L, B); put right with himself (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the legal word "justify". Readable says what it means: God puts a person right with him (meaning note m2).

decisions.choice: Gentiles ... nations
decisions.reason: English needs two words for the one Greek word; meaning note m4 shows they are the same.

decisions.choice: proclaimed the gospel beforehand (L); announced the gospel ahead of time (B); told the good news ahead of time (R)
decisions.reason: The verb contains the word for the gospel. Literal and Balanced say "gospel"; Readable says "good news", as it does for the noun.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}
decisions.reason: A pronoun for God follows the reader's setting.

decisions.choice: because of you
decisions.reason: Readable gives the plain sense of "in you" (meaning note m5).

records.source: ὥστε οἱ ἐκ πίστεως εὐλογοῦνται σὺν τῷ πιστῷ Ἀβραάμ.
records.gloss: So then those of faith are blessed with the believing Abraham.
pieces: So the people of faith share in the blessing together with Abraham, who believed.

L.9: So then those [who are] of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the believer.

R.9: So everyone who lives by faith is blessed together with Abraham, who believed God.

decisions.choice: believing: Abraham who trusted God
decisions.reason: πιστός can mean faithful or believing. Coming straight after "Abraham believed God" (verse 6), it points to his believing.

decisions.choice: with Abraham: sharing the one blessing given to him
alternatives: blessed in the same way as Abraham
decisions.reason: σύν means together with. Believers do not receive a blessing like his; they share the blessing God promised him (verse 8).

decisions.choice: lives by faith; believed God
decisions.reason: Readable explains the short phrases, as in verse 7.

records.source: Ὅσοι γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων νόμου εἰσὶν ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσίν, γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι Ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει πᾶσιν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ ποιῆσαι αὐτά.
records.gloss: As many as for of works of law are, under curse are; it has been written for: Cursed everyone who not remains in all the things having been written in the book of the law to do them.
pieces: For everyone whose standing rests on works of the law is under a curse. Scripture says, "A curse is on everyone who does not hold fast to everything written in the book of the law and do it."

L.10: For as many as are of works of [the] law are under a curse, for it is written, "Cursed [is] everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them."

R.10: People who depend on doing what the law commands are under a curse. Scripture says, "Everyone who does not keep on doing all that is written in the book of the law is under a curse."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Deuteronomy 27:26
decisions.reason: The words are from Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the curses announced when Israel entered the land, in the form of its Greek translation; "the book of the law" echoes Deuteronomy 28:58 and 29:20.

decisions.choice: a curse: God's judgment on those who break his covenant
decisions.reason: In Deuteronomy the law ends with blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience (Deuteronomy 27-28). The curse is the opposite of the blessing in verse 9.

decisions.choice: relying on the law brings a curse, because no one keeps all of it
alternatives: relying on the law is itself the curse, whether one keeps it or not
decisions.reason: Paul leaves a step unstated. The law curses everyone who does not do all it requires; no one does (2:16, 6:13); so those who look to the law for their standing with God fall under its curse. Others read the verse without that unstated step: the law's way of doing is itself not the way of faith (verse 12). Both readings agree that the law cannot bring the blessing.

decisions.choice: remain in: keep on obeying
decisions.reason: ἐμμένω means to stay with something, here to keep on doing all the law commands.

decisions.choice: of works of [the] law (L); whose standing rests on works of the law (B); depend on doing what the law commands (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what it means to be "of" works of the law: to look to them for one's standing with God.

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: The usual formula for quoting Scripture, put in plain English.

records.heading: Christ set us free from the curse

records.source: ὅτι δὲ ἐν νόμῳ οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται παρὰ τῷ θεῷ δῆλον, ὅτι Ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται, ὁ δὲ νόμος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ πίστεως, ἀλλ’· Ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: That and by law no one is justified before the God [is] evident, because: The righteous by faith will live; \v 12 the and law not is of faith, but: The [one] having done them will live by them.
pieces: It is plain that no one is justified in God's sight through the law, since "The one who is righteous will live by faith."
But the law does not rest on faith. Instead, "Whoever does these things will live by them."

L.11: And that no one is justified before God by [the] law [is] evident, because "The righteous [one] will live by faith."
L.12: But the law is not of faith; rather, "The one who does them will live by them."

R.11: It is clear that no one is put right with God by keeping the law. Scripture says, "Those who are righteous will live by faith."
R.12: But the law is not based on faith. The law says, "The person who does these things will live by doing them."

decisions.choice: it is evident that no one is justified by the law, because the righteous will live by faith
alternatives: because no one is justified by the law, it is evident that the righteous will live by faith
decisions.reason: The sentence has two ὅτι clauses, and either can go with "evident". We take the first: the quotation from Habakkuk is the proof. The other reading makes the quotation the conclusion. Both say that a right standing with God comes by faith, not by the law.

decisions.choice: God declares a person to be in the right before him: acquitted and accepted
alternatives: a person proves to be good
decisions.reason: δικαιόω is a word from the law court: the judge declares someone to be in the right. Here God is the judge, and the person he justifies is accepted by him and stands in the right before him (2:16). It is a verdict God gives, not a reward for good conduct.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Habakkuk 2:4
decisions.reason: The words come from Habakkuk 2:4, where God tells the prophet that the righteous will live by faith while the proud fail. The Hebrew has "by his faithfulness" and the Greek translation "by my faith"; Paul quotes it without either word, as he does in Romans 1:17.

decisions.choice: the righteous will live by faith
alternatives: the one who is righteous by faith will live
decisions.reason: The phrase "by faith" can go with "live" or with "the righteous". Paul's argument is about how a person comes to be in the right, so the second reading is possible; but the order of the words follows Habakkuk, where it goes with "live". The meaning is close either way: righteousness and life come by faith.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Leviticus 18:5
alternatives: Paul's own summary of the law
decisions.reason: Leviticus 18:5 promises life to the one who does God's statutes. Paul sets it beside Habakkuk 2:4 to show that the law works by doing, while life with God comes by faith (compare Romans 10:5).

decisions.choice: the law is not of faith: it works on the principle of doing
alternatives: the law is opposed to faith or is evil
decisions.reason: Paul is not saying the law is bad (verse 21). He is saying that the law's basis is doing what it commands, which is a different basis from believing.

decisions.choice: justified (L, B); put right with God (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the legal word. Readable says what it means (meaning note m2).

decisions.choice: by keeping the law; Scripture says; The law says; by doing them
decisions.reason: Readable says how the law could be thought to justify, names the source of each quotation, and makes the last words plain.

records.source: Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα, ὅτι γέγραπται· Ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου, ἵνα εἰς τὰ ἔθνη ἡ εὐλογία τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ γένηται ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἵνα τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ πνεύματος λάβωμεν διὰ τῆς πίστεως.
records.gloss: Christ us redeemed from the curse of the law, having become for us a curse, because it has been written: Cursed everyone the hanging on a tree, \v 14 so that to the Gentiles the blessing of the Abraham might come in Christ Jesus, so that the promise of the Spirit we might receive through the faith.
pieces: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse on our behalf, for it is written, "A curse is on everyone who is hung on a tree."
He did this so that in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus the blessing of Abraham would reach the Gentiles, and so that through faith we would receive the Spirit who was promised.

L.13: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written, "Cursed [is] everyone who hangs on a tree,"
L.14: so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

R.13: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} paid the price to set us free from the curse that the law brings. He did it by taking the curse on {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} for us. Scripture says, "Everyone who is hung on a tree is under a curse."
R.14: He did this so that the blessing God promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did it so that we would receive the Spirit God promised, through faith.

decisions.choice: redeemed: set free by paying the price
decisions.reason: ἐξαγοράζω means to buy out, as a slave or captive could be bought free. The price was Christ himself becoming a curse; Paul uses the same word for freedom from the law in 4:5.

decisions.choice: became a curse for us: took the curse on himself in our place
decisions.reason: ὑπὲρ means "on behalf of", and here what Christ did for us is to bear the curse that was ours. He became a curse in the sense that he came under the curse the law pronounces when he was hung on the cross; Paul says something similar in 2 Corinthians 5:21.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Deuteronomy 21:23
alternatives: a saying about crucifixion in general
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 21:23 says that the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree is cursed by God. Paul applies it to the cross, a wooden post. He quotes it in the same form as the curse in verse 10, so that the two curses meet.

decisions.choice: us: Jewish believers under the law first, and through them all who believe
alternatives: all believers, Jews and Gentiles alike, from the start
decisions.reason: Only those under the law were directly under its curse, and verse 14 turns to "the Gentiles" as a second group. Yet the "we" who receive the Spirit at the end of verse 14 includes the Galatians, who were Gentiles (4:5-6 has the same movement). The evidence is close.

decisions.choice: two purposes: the blessing for the Gentiles, and the Spirit for us
alternatives: the second purpose depends on the first
decisions.reason: Both clauses begin with "so that" and give what Christ's death achieved. The blessing promised to Abraham (verse 8) and the gift of the Spirit (verse 2) are two sides of the same result.

decisions.choice: the promise of the Spirit: the promised Spirit
alternatives: a promise that the Spirit makes
decisions.reason: The Spirit is what was promised (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28). Paul thus ties the blessing of Abraham to the gift of the Spirit the Galatians received by faith (verses 2-5).

decisions.choice: the promise of the Spirit
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads "promise". A few early manuscripts read "blessing", which repeats the word from earlier in the verse. Reviewers should check the apparatus before this sentence is marked reviewed.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting; at the start of a sentence "The Messiah".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Pronouns for Christ follow the reader's setting.

decisions.choice: tree
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy speaks of a tree, and Paul keeps the word to make the link with the cross clear without naming it.

decisions.choice: He did this (B, R); paid the price; the blessing God promised to Abraham (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced starts a new sentence at verse 14 and says what the purpose clauses depend on. Readable explains "redeemed" and "the blessing of Abraham" (meaning notes m1 and m6).

records.source: Ἀδελφοί, κατὰ ἄνθρωπον λέγω· ὅμως ἀνθρώπου κεκυρωμένην διαθήκην οὐδεὶς ἀθετεῖ ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεται.
records.gloss: Brothers, according to man I speak; even of man having been ratified covenant no one sets aside or adds to.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I will use an illustration from human life. Even a human will, once it has been made binding, is something no one can cancel or add new terms to.

L.15: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I speak in human terms: even a human covenant, once it has been ratified, no one sets aside or adds to.

R.15: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, here is an example from ordinary life. When someone makes a will and it has been made official, no one can cancel it or add anything to it.

decisions.choice: I speak in human terms: an illustration drawn from everyday human dealings
alternatives: I speak as a mere man would, without authority
decisions.reason: The phrase introduces a comparison from ordinary life, as in Romans 3:5 and 6:19. Paul is not lowering his authority; he is arguing from how people treat a binding document to how God treats his own promise.

decisions.choice: a will, the everyday sense of the word, chosen because the same word is the Scriptures' word for God's covenant
alternatives: a covenant or agreement between people
decisions.reason: διαθήκη was the ordinary Greek word for a will or testament, a binding arrangement made by one person about what others will receive. The Greek Scriptures use the same word for God's covenant with Abraham, and Paul uses it in that sense in verse 17, where it is "ratified beforehand by God". The talk of inheritance (verse 18) and heirs (verse 29) fits a will. But a will could normally be changed by the one who made it, so some read the word here as a human agreement or covenant, which neither party may change alone. Either way the point is the same: once in force it stands.

decisions.choice: sets aside or adds to: annul it or add new terms to it
decisions.reason: ἀθετέω means to declare void. ἐπιδιατάσσομαι, found only here in the New Testament, means to add further provisions. Paul has in view the law of Moses, which in his argument would be such an added provision if it changed the terms of the promise (verse 17).

decisions.choice: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, women and men, and in verse 28 says that in Christ there is "male and female" alike. "Brothers" stays available as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: covenant (L); will (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the word that verse 17 needs, so the reader can see that it is the same word. Balanced and Readable use the sense that the illustration has in ordinary life (meaning note m2), and verse 17 returns to "covenant" for God's arrangement with Abraham; the footnote tells the reader that one Greek word stands behind both.

decisions.choice: I will use an illustration from human life (B); here is an example from ordinary life (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek idiom says what kind of argument follows; Balanced and Readable say so in plain words.

records.heading: The law cannot cancel the promise

records.source: τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ ἐρρέθησαν αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ· οὐ λέγει· Καὶ τοῖς σπέρμασιν, ὡς ἐπὶ πολλῶν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐφ’ ἑνός· Καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σου, ὅς ἐστιν Χριστός.
records.gloss: And to Abraham were spoken the promises and to the seed of him. Not it says, And to the seeds, as of many, but as of one, And to the seed of you, who is Christ.
pieces: The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his descendant. Notice that Scripture does not say "and to descendants," as if many people were meant. It speaks of one: "and to your descendant," and that one is {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.16: Now to Abraham the promises were spoken, and to his seed. It does not say, "And to the seeds," as [referring] to many, but as [referring] to one, "And to your seed," who is {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.16: God spoke the promises to Abraham and to his descendant. Scripture does not say "descendants," as if it were talking about many people. It says "your descendant," which means one person, and that person is {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: "and to your seed": the promise to Abraham in Genesis
alternatives: a quotation of one verse only
decisions.reason: The words come from God's promises to Abraham, repeated several times: Genesis 13:15, 17:8 and 24:7 (compare 12:7 and 22:18). That is why Paul speaks of "the promises" in the plural. The land and the blessing were promised both to Abraham and to his descendants.

decisions.choice: the singular "seed" points to one descendant, Christ, in whom all his people are included
alternatives: Paul denies that the word can mean many descendants
a play on words with no real argument
decisions.reason: σπέρμα is a collective noun: in Genesis it means all of Abraham's descendants, and Paul knows this, for in verse 29 he calls the Galatian believers Abraham's "seed". His point is that the promise always looked to one line, and in the end to one person, the Messiah, through whom the blessing reaches the nations (3:14). Those who belong to Christ are counted as the seed because they are in him (verse 29). The plural σπέρμασιν is an unusual form, used here to make the contrast.

decisions.choice: it says: Scripture, through which God speaks
alternatives: he says, with God as the subject
decisions.reason: λέγω has no stated subject. In 3:8 Paul speaks of Scripture foreseeing and announcing, and in 3:22 of Scripture shutting up all things; the subject here is Scripture or God speaking in it, which comes to the same.

decisions.choice: seed (L); descendant (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Seed" keeps the old picture and the singular form of the Greek. In modern English it is rarely used for people, so Balanced and Readable use a plain word for a person's children and their line. Here they need one that has a separate singular and plural (r-en-5).

decisions.choice: Scripture
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject the Greek leaves understood (meaning note m3).

decisions.choice: God spoke the promises
decisions.reason: Readable turns the passive into an active verb and names God, who made the promises.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

decisions.choice: descendant / descendants
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Balanced and Readable say "offspring", but in English that word is the same in the singular and the plural, so it cannot show the contrast Paul draws here between one and many. "Descendant" and "descendants" can.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ λέγω· διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ μετὰ τετρακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη γεγονὼς νόμος οὐκ ἀκυροῖ, εἰς τὸ καταργῆσαι τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν.
records.gloss: This and I say: covenant having been ratified beforehand by the God, the after four hundred and thirty years having come law not annuls, so as to nullify the promise.
pieces: My point is this. God had already ratified a covenant, and the law, coming 430 years afterward, cannot overturn it and so cancel the promise.

L.17: And this I say: a covenant ratified beforehand by God, the law that came 430 years afterward does not annul, so as to make the promise void.

R.17: This is what I mean. God made a covenant with Abraham and made it binding. The law came 430 years later. It cannot cancel that covenant and so do away with what God promised.

decisions.choice: God's covenant with Abraham, already made binding before the law
decisions.reason: The same word as in verse 15 now names God's own arrangement with Abraham (Genesis 15:18; 17:1-8). The prefix in προκυρόω means "ratified beforehand": it was in force long before Sinai.

decisions.choice: 430 years: the period Exodus gives for Israel's stay before the exodus
alternatives: an exact count from Abraham to Sinai
decisions.reason: Exodus 12:40-41 gives 430 years for Israel's time in Egypt; the Greek Old Testament counts the same 430 years for the time in Canaan and Egypt together. Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 round it to 400. Paul uses the familiar figure to say the law came long after the promise.

decisions.choice: so as to make the promise void: what annulling the covenant would amount to
alternatives: the law's purpose was to cancel the promise
decisions.reason: The construction gives the result that would follow if the law annulled the covenant. Paul denies both: the law does not annul the covenant, so it does not make the promise void.
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in figures.

decisions.choice: a covenant with Abraham
decisions.reason: Readable names the other party, whom verses 16 and 18 name, so the reader knows which covenant is meant.

decisions.choice: a covenant ... the law ... does not annul
alternatives: the law does not annul a covenant
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order, which puts the covenant first for emphasis.

records.source: εἰ γὰρ ἐκ νόμου ἡ κληρονομία, οὐκέτι ἐξ ἐπαγγελίας· τῷ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ δι’ ἐπαγγελίας κεχάρισται ὁ θεός.
records.gloss: If for from law the inheritance, no longer from promise; but to Abraham through promise has granted the God.
pieces: For if the inheritance depends on the law, it no longer depends on a promise. But God gave it freely to Abraham by means of a promise.

L.18: For if the inheritance [is] from [the] law, [it is] no longer from promise; but to Abraham God has freely given [it] through promise.

R.18: If the inheritance came from keeping the law, it would no longer come from a promise. But God gave it to Abraham as a gift, by promising it.

decisions.choice: the inheritance: what God promised to give Abraham and his offspring
decisions.reason: In Genesis the inheritance was the land (Genesis 15:7; 17:8). In Galatians Paul widens it to all that God promised: the blessing of Abraham and the Spirit (3:14), sonship (4:7) and the kingdom of God (5:21).

decisions.choice: from law, from promise: the law and the promise as two different grounds
alternatives: the inheritance can rest on both together
decisions.reason: Paul sets the two against each other: if the inheritance depends on keeping the law, it no longer rests on a promise, because a promise is kept by the one who makes it, while the law depends on what people do (3:12).

decisions.choice: has given freely, as a gift, and the gift still stands
alternatives: has granted as a right earned
decisions.reason: χαρίζομαι comes from the same root as the word for grace: it means to give as a favor. The perfect tense says that the gift given to Abraham remains in force.

decisions.choice: from keeping the law
decisions.reason: Readable says how the inheritance would come from the law: by doing what it commands.

decisions.choice: freely given (L); gave it freely (B); gave it ... as a gift (R)
decisions.reason: "Granted" loses the note of free favor in the Greek verb (meaning note m3).

records.source: Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος;
records.gloss: What then the law?
pieces: What, then, was the law for?

R.19: Then what was the purpose of the law?

decisions.choice: why the law: what was its purpose
decisions.reason: The question has no verb. After verses 15-18 have shown that the law cannot add to or cancel the promise, the natural question is what it was for, and the answer that follows gives its purpose and its time limit.

decisions.choice: was ... for (B); was the purpose of (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb the Greek leaves out and make the question a question about purpose.

records.heading: Why the law was given

records.source: τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη, ἄχρις οὗ ἔλθῃ τὸ σπέρμα ᾧ ἐπήγγελται, διαταγεὶς δι’ ἀγγέλων ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου·
records.gloss: Of the transgressions because of it was added, until should come the seed to whom it has been promised, having been ordered through angels by hand of a mediator.
pieces: It was added because of transgressions, and only until the offspring should come, the one to whom the promise was made. Angels set it in order, and it came through the hand of a mediator.

L.19: It was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed would come to whom [the promise] has been made, being ordered through angels by [the] hand of a mediator.

R.19: It was added because of wrongdoing, and it was meant to last only until the offspring came, the one God's promise was about. God gave the law through angels, and it was handed on by a go-between, Moses.

decisions.choice: because of transgressions: to bring them to light as the breaking of a clear command
alternatives: to hold back sin until Christ came
decisions.reason: χάριν after a noun means "for the sake of" or "because of" and does not say how. παράβασις is the stepping over of a known command. Romans 4:15 and 5:20 suggest that the law made wrongdoing visible as transgression; the picture of the guardian in verses 23-24 suggests that it also held sin in check. The text leaves both possible.

decisions.choice: until the offspring came: the law was given for a limited time
alternatives: until the end of the world
decisions.reason: The law had a beginning (430 years after the promise, verse 17) and an end, the coming of the one offspring, Christ (verse 16). Verses 23-25 make the same point with the picture of the guardian.

decisions.choice: angels and a mediator: the giving of the law at Sinai through angels and Moses
decisions.reason: Jewish tradition held that angels were present when the law was given (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek Old Testament; Acts 7:38, 53; Hebrews 2:2). The mediator is Moses, who stood between the Lord and the people (Deuteronomy 5:5). Paul's point is that the law came at one remove, while the promise was spoken by God himself (verse 18).

decisions.choice: seed (L); offspring (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16.

decisions.choice: God's promise; God gave the law; Moses
alternatives: the promise was made; it was ordered; a mediator
decisions.reason: Readable names the one who promised and gave the law, and the mediator, whom meaning note m3 identifies.

decisions.choice: wrongdoing
decisions.reason: Readable uses a common word; Literal and Balanced keep "transgressions", the breaking of a command.

records.source: ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν, ὁ δὲ θεὸς εἷς ἐστιν.
records.gloss: The but mediator of one not is, the but God one is.
pieces: Now a mediator does not act for one party alone, but God is one.

L.20: Now the mediator is not of one, but God is one.

R.20: A go-between always stands between two sides, but God is one.

decisions.choice: a mediator stands between parties, but the promise came straight from the one God
alternatives: God is one, so the law and the promise cannot conflict
the one God is the God of Jews and Gentiles alike (Romans 3:29-30)
decisions.reason: This is one of the hardest sentences in Paul's letters, and it has been read in very many ways. The reading followed here takes it with verse 19: the law came through a go-between, which implies two parties, God and Israel, with angels between; the promise was given to Abraham directly by God, who is one and acts alone.

decisions.choice: God is one: an echo of the Shema
decisions.reason: "God is one" recalls the confession of Israel in Deuteronomy 6:4. Paul uses the same words in Romans 3:30.

decisions.choice: does not act for one party alone (B); stands between two sides (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek is compressed; Balanced and Readable say what "not of one" means about a mediator.

records.source: Ὁ οὖν νόμος κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ;
records.gloss: The then law against the promises of the God?
pieces: Does the law, then, oppose God's promises?

L.21: [Is] the law then against the promises of God?

R.21: Does this mean that the law is against God's promises?

decisions.choice: of God: read
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts, among them the oldest papyrus of Paul's letters and Codex Vaticanus, leave out "of God". The SBLGNT keeps the words, and the sense is the same either way: the promises are God's.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
decisions.reason: If the law was added later and came through a go-between, a reader might think it works against the promise. Paul raises the objection in order to reject it.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· εἰ γὰρ ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζῳοποιῆσαι, ὄντως ἐκ νόμου ἂν ἦν ἡ δικαιοσύνη.
records.gloss: Not may it be! If for was given law the being able to make alive, really from law would have been the righteousness.
pieces: Certainly not! Had any law been given with the power to make people alive, then righteousness would in fact come by way of the law.

L.21: May it not be! For if a law had been given that was able to give life, righteousness would truly have been from [the] law.

R.21: Of course not! If God had given a law that had the power to give life, then righteousness really would come from keeping the law.

decisions.choice: a strong rejection: certainly not
alternatives: a wish: may it not happen
decisions.reason: μὴ γένοιτο is Paul's usual way of rejecting a wrong conclusion (2:17; Romans 3:4, 6:2).

decisions.choice: give life: the life God gives, which the law cannot give
decisions.reason: ζῳοποιέω is giving life to the dead (Romans 4:17; 8:11). Paul has quoted "the righteous will live by faith" (3:11); the law can command but cannot give that life. Compare 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the Spirit gives life".

decisions.choice: righteousness: being in the right before God
decisions.reason: As in 2:21, righteousness is the standing God gives, the result of being justified (verse 24). If the law could give life, it could give this standing too; but it cannot.

decisions.choice: If God had given; from keeping the law
alternatives: if a law had been given; from the law
decisions.reason: Readable names the giver and says how righteousness would come from the law.

decisions.choice: May it not be! (L); Certainly not! (B); Of course not! (R)
decisions.reason: Each level gives the force of the strong rejection in its own register; "God forbid" adds a name the Greek does not have.

records.source: ἀλλὰ συνέκλεισεν ἡ γραφὴ τὰ πάντα ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν ἵνα ἡ ἐπαγγελία ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δοθῇ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν.
records.gloss: But shut up the Scripture the all things under sin, so that the promise from faith of Jesus Christ might be given to the ones believing.
pieces: But Scripture has locked up everything under the power of sin, so that what was promised might be given, on the ground of faith in Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, to those who believe.

L.22: But the Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise, from faith in Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, might be given to those who believe.

R.22: But Scripture has shut up everyone and everything as prisoners under sin. It did this so that the promise would be given, through faith in Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, to those who believe.

decisions.choice: Scripture declared all people prisoners of sin
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of Scripture acting, as in 3:8, because what Scripture says is God's verdict. Passages such as Deuteronomy 27:26, quoted in 3:10, and those gathered in Romans 3:10-18 declare everyone guilty. Romans 11:32 uses the same verb of God: he has shut up all in disobedience, so that he may have mercy on all.

decisions.choice: all things: the whole human race and its world
decisions.reason: The neuter "all things" is all-inclusive. Paul means Jews and Gentiles alike, as in Romans 3:9, "all are under sin".

decisions.choice: faith in Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: With a person's name after it, πίστις can mean faith that person has or faith directed to that person. Read the second way, Paul means the believer's faith in Jesus Christ. Read the first way, he means Christ's own faithfulness to God, shown in his obedience to the cross, and "those who believe" at the end of the verse is the human answer to it. For "faith in Christ": the same verse goes on to speak of believing, and in 2:16 the same kind of phrase sits beside "we too have believed in Christ Jesus". For "faithfulness of Christ": the verse would otherwise name the believer's faith twice, and verses 23 and 25 speak of faith "coming" as an event in history, which suits Christ's own faithfulness. Both readings agree that the promise is given through Christ and not through the law. We follow the first and give the second in a footnote, as in Philippians 3:9.

decisions.choice: under the power of sin (B); as prisoners under sin (R)
decisions.reason: "Under sin" means under sin's rule (Romans 3:9; 7:14); Balanced says so, and Readable keeps the picture of the verb, shutting in like prisoners.

decisions.choice: what was promised
decisions.reason: The promise here is what was promised, the gift itself (3:14), which is given to believers.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

records.source: Πρὸ τοῦ δὲ ἐλθεῖν τὴν πίστιν ὑπὸ νόμον ἐφρουρούμεθα συγκλειόμενοι εἰς τὴν μέλλουσαν πίστιν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι.
records.gloss: Before the and to come the faith, under law we were being guarded, being shut up for the being about faith to be revealed.
pieces: Until faith came, the law held us in custody. We were kept shut in, waiting for the faith that was going to be revealed.

L.23: Now before the faith came, we were kept under guard under [the] law, being shut up for the faith that was about to be revealed.

R.23: Before the time of faith came, the law kept us under guard like prisoners. We were shut in until the faith that was coming would be made known.

decisions.choice: the faith: faith in Christ as a new stage in God's plan, which came and was revealed
alternatives: the Christian faith as a body of teaching
decisions.reason: Abraham believed long before (3:6), so Paul does not mean that no one had faith before Christ. With the article he speaks of faith as something that "came" and "was revealed" at a set time, when Christ came (verses 24-25; 4:4). Faith here stands for the new way God deals with people in Christ.

decisions.choice: kept under guard: held in custody, guarded and confined
decisions.reason: φρουρέω is used of guarding a city or keeping watch over prisoners (2 Corinthians 11:32); συγκλείω repeats the "shutting up" of verse 22. The picture is mainly of confinement, but the next verse's guardian shows that the custody had a good purpose and an end.

decisions.choice: we: Paul and his fellow Jews, who lived under the law
decisions.reason: "Under the law" fits Israel first. But in 4:3-9 Paul says that Gentiles too were enslaved before Christ, and in 3:26 he moves to "you all", so the "we" may already include them.

decisions.choice: the law held us in custody (B); the law kept us under guard (R)
alternatives: we were held in custody under the law
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the law the subject of an active verb, which reads more plainly in English.

decisions.choice: the time of faith
decisions.reason: Readable says that the coming of faith is a time in God's plan (meaning note m1).

records.heading: No longer under a guardian

records.source: ὥστε ὁ νόμος παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν γέγονεν εἰς Χριστόν, ἵνα ἐκ πίστεως δικαιωθῶμεν·
records.gloss: So that the law guardian of us has become unto Christ, so that from faith we might be justified.
pieces: In this way the law served as our guardian until the coming of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, so that faith would be the way we are justified.

L.24: So the law has become our guardian until {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, so that we might be justified by faith.

R.24: So the law was like a guardian, the servant who was put in charge of a child, until {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} came. Then we could be put right with God by faith.

decisions.choice: guardian: the household slave who watched over a boy until he came of age
alternatives: a schoolmaster or tutor who taught him
decisions.reason: In Greek and Roman homes the παιδαγωγός was a slave who looked after a boy from early childhood until his teens: he took him to school, kept him from trouble and corrected him. He was not the teacher. Paul's point is that the law had charge of God's people for a limited time, like a child who is not yet an heir in full (4:1-2).

decisions.choice: until Christ: the guardian's time lasted until Christ came
decisions.reason: εἰς can mean "until" or "to, leading to". Verses 23 and 25 are about time, before faith came and after, so "until Christ" fits the passage best. The older reading, that the law led people to Christ, is true to what Paul says elsewhere of the law, but does not seem to be his point here.

decisions.choice: justified: declared by God to be in the right before him, acquitted and accepted
alternatives: treated as if righteous with no real change of standing
decisions.reason: δικαιόω is a law-court word: the judge declares someone in the right. In Galatians God is the judge, and those he justifies are acquitted and accepted as his own (2:16; 3:8, 11). The life of the Spirit follows from this, but the word itself names God's verdict.

decisions.choice: be put right with God (R); be justified (L, B)
decisions.reason: "Justify" is a key word of the letter and stays at Literal and Balanced. Readable says what it means in plain words: put right with God, the one who gives the verdict.

decisions.choice: like a guardian, the servant who was put in charge of a child
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the guardian was (meaning note m1), since English has no single word for him. It says "servant", as the style guide has it; m1 keeps that he was a household slave.

decisions.choice: until the coming of Christ (B); until Christ came (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the time meaning of "until Christ" (meaning note m2).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

records.source: ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς πίστεως οὐκέτι ὑπὸ παιδαγωγόν ἐσμεν.
records.gloss: Having come and the faith, no longer under guardian we are.
pieces: Faith has now come, and we are no longer in the care of a guardian.

L.25: But the faith having come, we are no longer under a guardian.

R.25: But now the time of faith has come, and we are not under that guardian any longer.

decisions.choice: now that faith has come: the time of the guardian is over
alternatives: whenever a person comes to faith
decisions.reason: The words take up "before the faith came" in verse 23: the coming of faith is the arrival of Christ in history, and with it the end of the law's role as guardian. Each believer enters that new time by faith (verse 26).

decisions.choice: the time of faith
decisions.reason: As in verse 23.

decisions.choice: in the care of a guardian
decisions.reason: The guardian was a carer and supervisor (verse 24, meaning note m1); Balanced says what being "under" him meant.

records.source: πάντες γὰρ υἱοὶ θεοῦ ἐστε διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: All for sons of God you are through the faith in Christ Jesus.
pieces: For in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus you are all {{gender:children|sons}} of God, through faith.

L.26: For you are all {{gender:children|sons}} of God through the faith, in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.26: All of you are God's {{gender:children|sons}} through faith, because you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: sons of God: the status of a son and heir, given to women and men alike
alternatives: children in a general sense, without the right of the heir
decisions.reason: In Paul's world it was the son who inherited, and the word carries that status: verse 29 calls these sons "heirs", and 4:1-7 develops the picture. Paul gives this status to all believers, since in Christ there is "male and female" alike (verse 28). The Greek word is masculine, but its point is the standing of the heir, not the sex of the believer.

decisions.choice: in Christ Jesus goes with "you are sons": you are God's sons in union with Christ, through faith
alternatives: faith in Christ Jesus, with Christ as the one believed in
decisions.reason: Paul rarely uses "in" for the one in whom faith is placed. The next two verses speak of being baptized into Christ and of being one "in Christ Jesus", so here too "in Christ Jesus" most likely says where believers are: joined to him. Faith is the means, union with Christ the place.

decisions.choice: you all: Paul turns from "we" to "you", including the Gentile believers of Galatia
decisions.reason: After "we" in verses 23-25, Paul now addresses the Galatians directly. Gentiles who were never under the law are God's sons on the same footing.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The default is inclusive, because Paul applies the status to all believers (meaning note m1); "sons" keeps the word of the heir. The footnote explains the difference.

decisions.choice: in Christ Jesus placed first
decisions.reason: Putting "in Christ Jesus" first keeps it from being read as the object of faith (meaning note m2).

decisions.choice: because you belong to Christ Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says what being "in" Christ means here: joined to him and belonging to him (verse 29).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

records.source: ὅσοι γὰρ εἰς Χριστὸν ἐβαπτίσθητε, Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε·
records.gloss: As many as for into Christ you were baptized, Christ you put on.
pieces: Every one of you who was baptized into {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has put on {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} like clothing.

L.27: For as many [of you] as were baptized into {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, you clothed yourselves with {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.27: All of you who were baptized and joined to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} have put on {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, like a set of new clothes.

decisions.choice: baptized into Christ: baptized into union with him
alternatives: baptized in the name of Christ only
decisions.reason: Baptism "into" Christ marks the start of belonging to him and sharing in his death and life (Romans 6:3-4; 1 Corinthians 12:13). It explains how believers come to be "in Christ Jesus" (verse 26).

decisions.choice: put on Christ: take him on like a garment, so that one's identity is his
decisions.reason: To "put on" a person was to take on that person's character and role. Paul uses the picture for what happened at baptism, and also calls believers to live it out (Romans 13:14; compare Colossians 3:9-10). The clothing image leads into verse 28: under the one garment the old marks of standing no longer divide.

decisions.choice: like clothing (B); like a set of new clothes (R)
decisions.reason: "Put on Christ" is unclear in modern English; the comparison makes the picture plain.

decisions.choice: baptized and joined to Christ
decisions.reason: Readable explains "into" (meaning note m1).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

records.source: οὐκ ἔνι Ἰουδαῖος οὐδὲ Ἕλλην, οὐκ ἔνι δοῦλος οὐδὲ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ· πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: Not there is Jew nor Greek, not there is slave nor free, not there is male and female; all for you one are in Christ Jesus.
pieces: There is no Jew or Greek, there is no slave or free person, there is no male and female, for all of you are one in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.28: There is not Jew nor Greek, there is not slave nor free, there is not male and female; for all you are one in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.28: Being a Jew or a Gentile, a slave or a free person, a man or a woman, does not divide you. All of you are one in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.choice: in Christ these distinctions give no one a different standing: all are one
alternatives: the differences themselves cease to exist
a statement about spiritual equality with no effect on how believers live together
decisions.reason: The three pairs were the great divisions of the ancient world, by race, by social position and by sex. In Christ none of them gives anyone a higher or lower place among God's children and heirs (verses 26 and 29). Paul still speaks to Jews and Gentiles, slaves and masters, men and women as such (1 Corinthians 7:17-24), but in Galatians the first pair has direct consequences: Gentiles need not become Jews, and Jewish believers may not separate from them at the table (2:11-14). Colossians 3:11 has a similar list.

decisions.choice: male and female: the words of Genesis 1:27
decisions.reason: The first two pairs use "nor"; the third uses "and", the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament, "male and female he made them". The new creation in Christ (6:15) does not divide along the line drawn in the first creation.

decisions.choice: Greek: a Gentile, anyone who is not a Jew
decisions.reason: Paired with "Jew", Ἕλλην stands for all non-Jews, as in Romans 1:16. The Galatians themselves were not Greeks by birth.

decisions.choice: one: one person, one body, in Christ
decisions.reason: εἷς is masculine: believers are together one new person in Christ, the one offspring of Abraham (verses 16 and 29; compare Ephesians 2:15). Unity here is not agreement but belonging to one body.

decisions.choice: Gentile (R); Greek (L, B)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense the pair has (meaning note m3).

decisions.choice: does not divide you
decisions.reason: Readable says what "there is not" means for the church (meaning note m1); it does not say the differences have disappeared.

decisions.choice: a man or a woman
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for the pair; Literal and Balanced keep "male and female", which echo Genesis 1:27.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ὑμεῖς Χριστοῦ, ἄρα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ σπέρμα ἐστέ, κατ’ ἐπαγγελίαν κληρονόμοι.
records.gloss: If and you of Christ, then of the Abraham seed you are, according to promise heirs.
pieces: And if you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, it follows that you are Abraham's offspring, heirs in keeping with the promise.

L.29: And if you [are] of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, then you are Abraham's seed, heirs according to promise.

R.29: If you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, then you are Abraham's offspring too. You are heirs who will receive what God promised.

decisions.choice: belonging to Christ, the one seed, makes believers Abraham's seed
alternatives: believers become Abraham's descendants by physical birth or by circumcision
decisions.reason: In verse 16 the one seed is Christ. Those who belong to him are included in him, so they are Abraham's seed too, though many and though Gentiles. Paul keeps the singular σπέρμα with a plural "you": all of them together are the one offspring in Christ. This answers the claim that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong to Abraham's family.

decisions.choice: heirs: those who will receive the inheritance God promised
decisions.reason: The inheritance of verse 18 comes by promise, not by the law, and it goes to heirs. Paul develops the picture of the heir in 4:1-7.

decisions.choice: seed (L); offspring (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16.

decisions.choice: belong to Christ
decisions.reason: The genitive means belonging; Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: heirs who will receive what God promised
decisions.reason: Readable explains what an heir "according to promise" receives.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting: "Christ" by default, "Messiah" as the alternative.
